expectations.text: Documented boundaries are exercised as documented: ttl <= 0 stores without expiry, Get hides expired entries before the janitor sweeps, Close idempotence, the documented panic on non-positive janitor interval
expectations.evidence: ttl=0 entry "sess-b" is stored and shown to survive three sweeps (lines 49, 87-89); expiry-on-read is checked at 100ms against a 50ms TTL, well before the 1s sweep, for both Get and Len (lines 72-79); Close is called explicitly (line 95) with the deferred Close (line 45) as the proven-safe second call (line 106); New(0) and New(-time.Second) both must panic (lines 110-121). Note: only ttl=0 (the boundary value) exercises the ttl <= 0 clause; a negative ttl to Set is not separately exercised.

expectations.text: The package's DOCUMENTED concurrency safety is tested as promised (this package explicitly promises concurrent use, so concurrent exercise is in-contract), without statistical race-hunting theatrics
expectations.evidence: cache.go line 21 promises "All methods are safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines", making concurrent exercise in-contract, yet grep shows the test file spawns zero goroutines: no test ever calls Set/Get/Len/Close from more than one goroutine. The only concurrency exercised is the internal janitor interleaving with the single test goroutine inside the synctest bubble, which never exercises the multi-caller promise. report.md concedes the gap ("I skipped a race-hunt stressor since the docs' concurrency promise is covered by running the scenario under -race"), conflating a realistic in-contract concurrent exercise with race-hunting theatrics; the assertion asks for the former while forbidding only the latter. The -race pass (verified) therefore never observes two goroutines in the public API.

expectations.text: Comment discipline: NON-TRIVIAL tests carry a rationale doc comment in layman's terms; trivial ones may carry none; no comment opens with its own function name; no comment explains conventions, test ordering, synctest mechanics, or says a test 'pins the contract' (anti-slop)
expectations.evidence: The non-trivial TestCacheLifecycle carries a layman's rationale doc comment (lines 34-41, "One session token's whole life..."); the trivial panic test carries none. Neither test/example doc comment opens with its own function name (mustPanic's name-first comment is a plain helper following standard Go doc convention, outside the test-function rule). grep finds no 'pins', 'convention', or ordering talk; nothing explains synctest mechanics ('on virtual time' names the medium without explaining it).

expectations.text: Runnable examples speak to pkgsite users about the attributed symbol/scenario: the doc comment never narrates the code or addresses maintainers, and in-function comments explain non-obvious inputs and contract behavior at the call sites
